Shortly
SHORT-lee
adv.
From short, Saxon sceort, and the adverbial -ly. Webster 1828: quickly; soon; in a little time; also, briefly, in few words. Revelation opens with it, and how it is understood governs how the whole book is read.

Biblical Definition

Shortly in the New Testament is a word of imminence, and it appears at three very different scales. Of ordinary Christian travel: I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face (3 John 1:14) — a letter cut short because the writer expects to arrive. Of a man’s own approaching death, spoken with striking calm: Knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle, even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me (2 Peter 1:14). Of the promised crushing of the enemy: And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly (Romans 16:20) — the language of Genesis 3:15, and the bruising is under your feet, the church sharing the victory of its Head. And of the whole book of Revelation: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass (Revelation 1:1), repeated at the book’s close in Revelation 22:6. What John was shown was given to servants as things that must shortly come to pass, and the book ends Surely I come quickly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SHORTLY as quickly; soon; in a little time; and, in a second sense, briefly or in few words.

expand to see more

SHORTLY, adv. — Quickly; soon; in a little time; before long.

In few words; briefly; as, to state a matter shortly.

SHORT, a. — Not long; not extended in time or space; brief.

Applied in Scripture both to a near event and to the whole span of the present age as God measures it.

From Saxon sceort, short — the root also of shorten, shortage, and shirt.

Key Scripture

Revelation 1:1 — "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:"

Romans 16:20 — "And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen."

2 Peter 1:14 — "Knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle, even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me."

3 John 1:14 — "But I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. Peace be to thee. Our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name."

Modern Corruption

Full preterism takes shortly in Revelation 1:1 to mean that every prophecy in the book was fulfilled by AD 70, which requires the resurrection and the second coming to be past events and is therefore outside the bounds of orthodoxy.

expand to see more

The word does real work and cannot simply be spiritualised away; partial preterism, which reads much of Matthew 24 and parts of Revelation as fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem, is within Reformed orthodoxy and the dictionary treats it as such. What is not within orthodoxy is the full-preterist claim that all prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, including the resurrection of the body and the second coming. Paul names that error by its first-century form: Hymenaeus and Philetus, who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:18). Every creed the church has confessed looks forward to a bodily return and a bodily resurrection, and 1 Corinthians 15 makes the future resurrection of believers inseparable from the past resurrection of Christ.

The opposite error treats shortly and quickly as meaning nothing at all, so that the church settles into an indefinite present with no expectation. That is the mockery Peter answers — Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were — and his reply is not that the promise was figurative but that God measures time differently and is being patient. Romans 16:20 shows the pastoral use of the word: Paul tells a divided, harassed church that the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly, and it is offered as comfort in the middle of a warning about those who cause divisions. The nearness is meant to be felt.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek en tachei (G5034), in speed, shortly; tachu (G5035), quickly; tacheos (G5030), soon; syntemno (G4932), to cut short.

expand to see more

Greek en tachei (G5034) — with speed, shortly; things which must shortly come to pass (Revelation 1:1).

Greek tachu (G5035) — quickly; Surely I come quickly (Revelation 22:20).

Greek tacheos (G5030) — soon, hastily; shortly I must put off this my tabernacle (2 Peter 1:14).

Greek skenoma (G4638) — a tent, a tabernacle; Peter’s word for his own body.

Greek suntribo (G4937) — to crush, to break in pieces; shall bruise Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20).

Usage

"Things which must shortly come to pass (Revelation 1:1) — the word that governs how the book is read."

"The God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly (Romans 16:20) — Genesis 3:15, and under the church’s feet."

"Shortly I must put off this my tabernacle (2 Peter 1:14) — a man naming his own death with calm."
